The study introduces a rare double-ray phenomenon involving resonant light scattering from a periodic metasurface, designed to generate robust non-specular reflection. This metasurface consists of silicon nanodisk arrays positioned on a thin silica-on-metal substrate. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this structure enables low-loss, non-specular resonant reflection regardless of the incident wave's direction or polarization. The research details the requirements for achieving an autocollimation scattering scheme and observing non-specular reflected rays that fall outside the plane of incidence. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that adjusting the dielectric substrate thickness can tune the bandwidth of non-specular reflection. Finally, the intensity of both specular and non-specular reflected rays can be regulated by modifying the angle of incidence or the polarization state of the incoming wave.

This work introduces novel differential privacy frameworks designed for scenarios where data products must simultaneously satisfy external \emph{invariants} and \emph{integer} constraints. Such requirements are critical in real-world private data curation tasks, exemplified by the public release of the 2020 U.S. Decennial Census, yet they present significant obstacles to generating data products that are both provably private and statistically useful. To address this, we introduce \emph{integer subspace differential privacy}, a rigorous formulation for privacy guarantees when both invariants and integer properties are maintained, along with an analysis of its composition and post-processing properties. To overcome the difficulty of sampling from highly restricted discrete spaces, we develop two unbiased additive mechanisms—generalized Laplace and generalized Gaussian mechanisms—by solving the associated Diophantine equations. These mechanisms offer high accuracy, characterized by error distributions with sub-exponential and sub-Gaussian tail probabilities, respectively. For implementation, we created an MCMC algorithm and provided empirical convergence evaluations using estimated upper bounds on total variation distance derived from $L$-lag coupling. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through applications to a synthetic problem involving intersecting invariants, a sensitive contingency table with fixed margins, and 2010 Census county-level data subject to mandatory fixed state population totals.

Basic categories like "animal" or "furniture" are learned early in life and are essential for processing, organizing, and sharing knowledge about the world. These categories are universal across cultures, enabling efficient representation of worldly complexity and reflecting a shared mental representation within communities. However, current models of category learning and representation are typically evaluated using small-scale experiments with limited concepts and artificially constrained features, predominantly involving participants from specific cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds, often Western English speakers such as U.S. college students. This study investigates whether categorization models generalize (a) to rich, noisy data that mirrors the real-world human environment and (b) across different languages and cultures. We introduce a Bayesian cognitive model capable of jointly learning categories and their structured representations from natural language text, which facilitates (a) large-scale performance evaluation and (b) application across a diverse array of languages. Our findings demonstrate that meaningful categories encompassing hundreds of concepts and richly structured feature representations emerge across languages. This work highlights the potential of recent advancements in computational modeling and large-scale naturalistic datasets for cognitive science research.

Electronic Mott insulators have spurred significant research in condensed-matter physics because of their complex connection to high-temperature superconductivity. While Mott phases have recently been demonstrated in atomic systems for both fermions and bosons, a solid-state signature of a Mott insulator utilizing bosons has remained elusive. In this study, we reveal such a signature by investigating the Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian through semiconductor excitons trapped within two-dimensional lattices. We focus on the regime where on-site interactions are comparable to the energy spacing between confined lattice states. Our observations confirm that Mott phases are achievable, featuring uniform filling of lattice sites with up to two excitons. Furthermore, our technology enables the on-demand programming of the exciton-confining lattice geometry. This adaptability, coupled with the long-range dipolar interactions between excitons, opens a new pathway to investigate many-body phases that spontaneously break lattice symmetry.

This study examines exclusive $\pi^-\Delta^{++}$ electroproduction using the handbag framework, where helicity amplitudes decompose into hard partonic interactions and generalized parton distributions (GPDs). We introduce $p-\Delta$ transversity GPDs, adopting helicity non-flip GPDs from existing literature. To estimate observables numerically, we apply large-$N_C$ constraints to link specific $p-\Delta$ GPDs to proton-proton counterparts, disregarding others. Our calculation of twist-2 and twist-3 subprocess amplitudes incorporates quark transverse momenta alongside Sudakov suppressions, ultimately predicting partial cross sections for $\gamma^*p\to \pi^-\Delta^{++}$ within the large-$N_C$ limit.

Quantum walks serve as potent instruments for developing quantum search and sampling algorithms, specifically those designed to construct quantum stationary states. However, the success probabilities of these algorithms are significantly distant from unity. While amplitude amplification is typically employed to boost success rates, it introduces the "soufflé" problem. Achieving maximum probability requires stopping at the precise step; otherwise, increasing the step count can reduce success probability, creating practical challenges when the optimal step count is unknown. In this study, we introduce generalized interpolated quantum walks, capable of enhancing the success probability of search algorithms while circumventing the soufflé problem. By integrating generalized interpolated quantum walks with quantum fast-forwarding, we reduce the number of walk operator calls from $\Theta((\varepsilon^{-1})\sqrt{\Heg})$ to $\Theta(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})\sqrt{\Heg})$ and decrease the required ancilla qubits from $\Theta(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})+\log\sqrt{\Heg})$ to $\Theta(\log\log(\varepsilon^{-1})+\log\sqrt{\Heg})$. This combination improves success probability and eliminates the soufflé problem, where $\varepsilon$ represents precision and $\Heg$ denotes the classical hitting time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that generalized interpolated quantum walks can enhance the construction of quantum states corresponding to stationary distributions. Finally, we present an application utilizing generalized interpolated quantum walks to build a slowly evolving Markov chain sequence, a prerequisite for adiabatic stationary state preparation.

This study utilizes the functional renormalization group method to analyze a $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric gauge theory featuring a quiral superfield interacting with a vector $U(1)$ superfield. Our results confirm that the nonrenormalization theorem remains valid at the leading order of the supercovariant derivative expansion. Additionally, we derive the beta functions and examine the fixed point behavior under the local potential approximation, with a discussion on the employed regulators.

The lattice size $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$ of a lattice polytope $P$ serves as a crucial invariant; although it was formally defined to address bounds on the total and bi-degrees of algebraic curve equations, it has roots in earlier geometric combinatorics. This paper demonstrates that for any empty lattice polytope $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$, a reduced basis of $\mathbb{Z}^3$ exists that calculates $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$, thereby enabling an efficient algorithm for such computations. Furthermore, the findings are extended to another category of lattice width one polytopes within $\mathbb{R}^3$. Finally, a counterexample is presented to show that this property does not apply to all lattice width one lattice polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

In 2017, Colorado implemented risk-limiting tabulation audits (RLAs) statewide, utilizing both ballot-level comparison and ballot-polling techniques. However, these audits were limited to contests contained within a single county, as methods to efficiently audit cross-county contests that integrate both polling and comparison strategies were unavailable at the time. Consequently, Colorado's existing audit software (RLATool) required enhancements to handle contests spanning county boundaries and to process small contests more effectively. This paper addresses those gaps by introducing several approaches: extremely simple but inefficient methods, more efficient strategies combining ballot polling and ballot-level comparisons via stratified sampling, and techniques that merge ballot-level comparison with variable-size batch comparison without relying on stratified sampling. The authors conclude with specific recommendations and demonstrate their preferred method through examples that contrast it with current practices. Additionally, open-source code and interactive Jupyter notebooks are provided to implement these methods and facilitate further investigation.

Recent self-supervised approaches have achieved feature representations comparable to those from full supervision, offering benefits such as enhanced robustness and improved out-of-distribution detection. This paper presents an empirical investigation into how self-supervision, when used as a pre-training strategy or integrated into adversarial training, influences a model's resilience against $l_2$ and $l_{\infty}$ adversarial attacks as well as natural image corruptions. While self-supervision can boost robustness, the nuances of implementation are critical. Simply adding self-supervision loss alongside adversarial training improves accuracy only for perturbations smaller than or equal to the training budget ($\epsilon_{train}$); however, accuracy declines when evaluated on larger perturbations ($\epsilon_{test} \ge \epsilon_{train}$). Furthermore, increasing the weight of the self-supervision loss exacerbates this performance drop, ultimately harming robustness. We examine specific methods for integrating self-supervision into adversarial training and find that optimizing both network parameters and adversarial examples using self-supervised loss yields the most significant robustness gains, effectively acting as ensemble adversarial training. Although self-supervised pre-training offers advantages over random initialization for adversarial training, incorporating self-supervision directly into the adversarial training process provides no additional benefit to either model robustness or accuracy.

This note serves as a follow-up to Shu-Xue-Yao's work \cite{BYY}, which examined enhanced groups and associated dualities within type $A$. We extend this inquiry to explore enhanced dualities for classical groups of types $B$, $C$, and $D$. To achieve this, we first define an enhanced Brauer algebra. Leveraging Proposition \ref{B dual}, we readily derive restricted and Levi dualities, thereby naturally characterizing parabolic duality. Furthermore, explicit computations in Section \ref{3} present a specific instance.

Bayesian optimization typically requires an "inner optimization" step over a non-convex, highly multi-modal, and often non-differentiable data acquisition criterion, which can hinder standard local numerical optimizers. In these scenarios, it is standard practice to substitute continuous search with a discrete approach using randomly generated candidates. This paper proposes instead generating candidates derived from a Delaunay triangulation of the current input design. We outline the methodology for constructing these "tricands" and provide empirical evidence demonstrating that they surpass both numerically optimized acquisitions and random candidate alternatives. Furthermore, we show their suitability for hybrid schemes across various benchmark synthetic and real-world simulation experiments.

Recent research in quantum information science and technology has increasingly focused on control methods for three-level systems. This study presents numerical simulations of quantum process tomography for both STIRAP (stimulated Raman adiabatic passage) and saSTIRAP (superadiabatic STIRAP), utilizing realistic experimental parameters. We define an appropriate basis in operator space comprising the identity operator and the eight Gell-Mann operators to calculate the resulting $9 \times 9 = 81$-element process matrices. Our analysis covers both an ideal decoherence-free scenario and a more practical case that accounts for decoherence.

This document summarizes the most recent ATLAS experiment findings on top-quark pair production accompanied by a photon, utilizing proton-proton collision data from the LHC at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy. The results cover inclusive and differential cross-section measurements across single-lepton and dilepton final states, defined within a fiducial volume that matches the detector's acceptance.

We have discovered a novel cosmological signal, the Doppler-boosted Cosmic Infrared Background (DB-CIB), which originates from the peculiar motions of galaxies emitting thermal dust that constitutes the cosmic infrared background (CIB). This new observable serves as an independent probe of the cosmic velocity field and is closely analogous to the established kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect. Notably, DB-CIB avoids the "kSZ optical depth degeneracy," rendering it immune to the intricate astrophysics of galaxy formation. We predict that the DB-CIB effect will be detectable through cross-correlations between CCAT-Prime and DESI-like experiments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DB-CIB functions as a new CMB foreground that could bias future kSZ cross-correlations if not adequately accounted for.

Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes (MMDPs) serve as a robust framework for modeling sequential decision-making in cooperative multi-agent settings, with numerous centralized and decentralized planning algorithms developed to address them. However, the exponential growth of joint state and action spaces, combined with dynamic environmental changes, often hinders these methods from achieving both efficiency and scalability. While recent algorithms like the centralized FV-MCTS-MP and the decentralized *Alternate maximization with Behavioural Cloning* (ABC) have demonstrated strong performance, they fail to adapt to dynamic environments and manage inter-agent communication gaps, respectively. To address these limitations, we propose SiCLOP, a simulation-based online planning algorithm for cooperative multi-agent environments. SiCLOP integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with Coordination Graphs (CG) and Graph Neural Networks (GCN) to learn cooperation strategies and deliver real-time MMDP solutions. Furthermore, it enhances scalability via effective action space pruning. Unlike its predecessors, SiCLOP incorporates transfer learning, allowing agents to operate effectively across different environments. We also present a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence within multi-agent contexts. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that SiCLOP significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art online planning algorithms.

We introduce the 1-100 GeV spectral energy distribution (SED) for 148 recently identified high-synchrotron-peaked blazars (HSPs) from the First Brazil-ICRANet Gamma-ray Blazar catalogue (1BIGB) detected by Fermi-LAT. The majority of these 1BIGB sources are absent from prior Fermi-LAT catalogues, marking their initial presentation of gamma-ray spectral characteristics and significantly expanding the known gamma-ray blazar population. Given that the sample was initially selected based on excess signals within the 0.3-500 GeV range, these objects are promising candidates for very-high-energy (VHE) emission, potentially accessible to the upcoming CTA observatory. Our flux estimates utilize PASS8 data, integrating over more than nine years of Fermi-LAT observations. We also revisit the full broadband fit between 0.3-500 GeV originally detailed in the 1BIGB paper, updating the power-law parameters with the latest Fermi-LAT dataset. We evaluate the significance of these sources for VHE population studies involving both current facilities and the future CTA. To assess detectability, we select a subsample of 1BIGB sources, extrapolate their gamma-ray SEDs to higher energies while correcting for extragalactic background light absorption, and compare these extrapolations against published CTA sensitivity curves. Two specific sources, 1BIGB J224910.6-130002 and 1BIGB J194356.2+211821, receive detailed discussion. All gamma-ray SEDs, presented here for the first time, are made publicly accessible through the Brazilian Science Data Center (BSDC) service at CBPF in Rio de Janeiro.

This report outlines the findings of the Computational Frontier topical group regarding end-user analysis for Snowmass 2021. End-user analysis involves deriving physics results from reconstructed and simulated experimental data. High-energy physics experiments generate systems capable of performing shared reconstruction, calibration, and simulation tasks, which produce common data samples. These detailed samples are subsequently reduced into various analysis samples, often optimized for specific physics topics through trigger or data object selection. Analyzers (end users) then process these samples to generate physics results. Community consensus categorized the end-user analysis ensemble into five key areas: Analysis Ecosystems, Analysis Models, Dataset Bookkeeping and Formats, Collaborative Software, and Training. The following findings and recommendations address how these critical areas influence end-user analysis.

We establish that for smooth projective families of varieties with a good minimal model, the variation provides a lower bound for the base's Kodaira dimension when the base has dimension five or less and a non-negative Kodaira dimension. This result confirms the Kebekus-Kovacs conjecture for base spaces of dimension at most five.
